<br />
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
How to Live Life?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Tony E Hansen<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Reflection based upon Luke 6:27-38, Psalm 37; 1
Corinthians 15:35-50;<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Let our minds be in prayer. From the words of Psalm 19,
may the words of my mouth and the meditations of all of our hearts be acceptable
to you O God, You are our rock and you are our Redeemer!<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
People often drive on the highways with various
interpretations of what the signs on the road mean (Such as, speed limits.)
What is the legal definition of speed limit anyway?  Is it 5-over is the
speed limit posted, or is it conditions of the road?  What about stop
signs? Do you in fact stop on the line and wait? Do you creep up to the stop
and go if no one is looking? Do you just ignore that it is there?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Are these mere suggestions?  What happens when you
follow them to the letter?  What happens when you break these?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Even better question is what do other people see in your
example of these?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
We don’t get to read this sermon of the “level place” (or
the plain) often because we do not usually get a lengthy Epiphany like this
year. Today’s portion is a continuation of last week’s Scripture. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
There are similarities to the Sermon on the Mount in
Matthew. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
So let us walk through the text a bit here,<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
First, a recap of last week’s:<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Jesus is preaching to a crowd of people from Judea, Tyre
and Sidon (Jews and Gentiles). We have a version of the beatitudes.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Blessed are the poor, the hungry, and those who are
hurting. Blessed are those who hate you – especially on account of God. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Rejoice your day is coming!  You will have your
rewards.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
 Your efforts and toil will not go in vain, <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
but we have some Woes!<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
As in, don’t feel too safe in your material luxuries,
wealth, food, laughs or good reputation.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Ouch!  This is not an easy sermon to hear!  You
might look at yourself and wonder what am I missing. I feel ok, have food to
eat, laugh a good laugh and might even have a good name.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
In that part of the sermon, Jesus is describing something
that sounds reassuring to us who are suffering, but radical by challenging our
comfort zones just the same.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Now, today’s part of the lesson from Luke, we shift a bit
and we are given a set of precepts or teachings.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>You might even call these guides or rules,
and as rules and precepts go, these are pretty good ones on their face.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
To summarize today’s portion:<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Listen Now! <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Love your enemies.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Forgive those who hurt you.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Give to people.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
“do unto others as you would have them do to you.” <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Be fair in your work.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Be merciful.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Simple, but not as simple as we might like to think. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Then again, is being a Christian really simple?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Lets look at each of these for a moment.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<i style="mso-bidi-font-style: normal;">Listen Now!</i> <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
(In case, you were not listening before.)<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<i style="mso-bidi-font-style: normal;">Love your enemies.<o:p></o:p></i></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<i style="mso-bidi-font-style: normal;">Forgive those who
hurt you.<o:p></o:p></i></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
These two are difficult if you ever been on the receiving
end of bullying or prejudicial injustice.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;"> 
</span>I know this from personal experience.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<i style="mso-bidi-font-style: normal;">Give to people.<o:p></o:p></i></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
Here, I am reminded of my youth when our family didn’t
have much money and the church would give us those boxes and envelopes for us
kids to put money for the offering. When we would get a $5 in rare form, to
give a portion of that to the church was feeling “difficult.” <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<i style="mso-bidi-font-style: normal;">“do unto others as
you would have them do to you.”</i> <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
You might recognize this as the Golden rule, but as a
corollary to the earlier points, what happens when people are not nice or kind
to you?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">

How to Live Life? 
 
Tony E Hansen 
 

 
 
Reflection based upon Luke 6:27-38, Psalm 37; 1
Corinthians 15:35-50; 
 

 
 
Let our minds be in prayer. From the words of Psalm 19,
may the words of my mouth and the meditations of all of our hearts be acceptable
to you O God, You are our rock and you are our Redeemer! 
 

 
 
People often drive on the highways with various
interpretations of what the signs on the road mean (Such as, speed limits.)
What is the legal definition of speed limit anyway?  Is it 5-over is the
speed limit posted, or is it conditions of the road?  What about stop
signs? Do you in fact stop on the line and wait? Do you creep up to the stop
and go if no one is looking? Do you just ignore that it is there? 
 

 
 
Are these mere suggestions?  What happens when you
follow them to the letter?  What happens when you break these? 
 

 
 
Even better question is what do other people see in your
example of these? 
 

 
 
We don’t get to read this sermon of the “level place” (or
the plain) often because we do not usually get a lengthy Epiphany like this
year. Today’s portion is a continuation of last week’s Scripture.  
 

 
 
There are similarities to the Sermon on the Mount in
Matthew. 
 

 
 
So let us walk through the text a bit here, 
 

 
 
First, a recap of last week’s: 
 
Jesus is preaching to a crowd of people from Judea, Tyre
and Sidon (Jews and Gentiles). We have a version of the beatitudes. 
 

 
 
Blessed are the poor, the hungry, and those who are
hurting. Blessed are those who hate you – especially on account of God.  
 
Rejoice your day is coming!  You will have your
rewards. 
 
 Your efforts and toil will not go in vain, 
 
but we have some Woes! 
 
As in, don’t feel too safe in your material luxuries,
wealth, food, laughs or good reputation. 
 

 
 
Ouch!  This is not an easy sermon to hear!  You
might look at yourself and wonder what am I missing. I feel ok, have food to
eat, laugh a good laugh and might even have a good name. 
 

 
 
In that part of the sermon, Jesus is describing something
that sounds reassuring to us who are suffering, but radical by challenging our
comfort zones just the same. 
 

 
 
Now, today’s part of the lesson from Luke, we shift a bit
and we are given a set of precepts or teachings.   You might even call these guides or rules,
and as rules and precepts go, these are pretty good ones on their face. 
 

 
 
To summarize today’s portion: 
 
Listen Now! 
 
Love your enemies. 
 
Forgive those who hurt you. 
 
Give to people. 
 
“do unto others as you would have them do to you.” 
 
Be fair in your work. 
 
Be merciful. 
 

 
 
Simple, but not as simple as we might like to think. 
 
Then again, is being a Christian really simple? 
 

 
 
Lets look at each of these for a moment. 
 
 Listen Now! 
 
(In case, you were not listening before.) 
 
 Love your enemies. 
 
 Forgive those who
hurt you. 
 
These two are difficult if you ever been on the receiving
end of bullying or prejudicial injustice.  
 I know this from personal experience. 
 
 Give to people. 
 
Here, I am reminded of my youth when our family didn’t
have much money and the church would give us those boxes and envelopes for us
kids to put money for the offering. When we would get a $5 in rare form, to
give a portion of that to the church was feeling “difficult.” 
 
 “do unto others as
you would have them do to you.” 
 
You might recognize this as the Golden rule, but as a
corollary to the earlier points, what happens when people are not nice or kind
to you? 
 
 Be fair in your
work. 
 
 Be merciful. 
 
These are good things to be fair and merciful. 
 

 
 
Jesus challenges us and goes further in telling us to do these
(not just our friends, family and good neighbors, but) for any and every one.
(32) “If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even
sinners love those who love them.” 
 

 
 
There is a lot here! You might see yourself in many of
these in your own ways. 
 
Just like the road signs, There are a number of ways that
people come to the text of the Bible and these Gospels.  
 

 
 
Some of us read this as the rulebook for daily
living.  Some of us might read this text and say, “yeah that’s me!” Some
might say, “I am already saved – what more do I need?” Some of us read this
text and say, “um I have some work to do.”  You might count me in the
latter of that. 
 

 
 
If this is a rulebook, do you follow it and what does it
mean to follow these? 
 
Jesus presents to us a set of precepts and rules, and as
rules and precepts go these are pretty good ones and pretty radical because
Jesus tells us not to feel too comfortable in our comfort.   
 

 
 
Regardless of where you are on life’s journey (or if you
think you have done enough), Jesus does not distinguish for whom these precepts
are meant.  These are for us to follow and to live yes, but you might even
ask, why do we have to do this. That is a great question. 
 

 
 
Sure, we can be ethical in all of our work and have
morals action and thought, but still the question remains why do have to do
this? 
 

 
 
Be fair in your work. 
 
Be merciful. 
 
Why do we do this? Look at that last line, Because your
God is merciful. 
 

 
 
That’s right! This is not about you, this is describing
what God does for us and that is why we need to be like God. The world will
bless us in turn. Karma from God. 
 

 
 
That is big! Are these mere suggestions and rules, like
the road signs?   
 

 
 
I submit to you there is something more than just
following a law, but as one writer describes, these first parts (the blessed
are the hungry, the poor and the hurting and woe if you revel in your luxuries)
these, along with karma, outline the reward of God’s kingdom.   Then this set of precepts outlines how we
participate in that kingdom today and now. 
 

 
 
So then the question changes from whether you follow
these or not – into “How do we reveal that in our lives?”  How do we
reveal God’s kingdom in the now, here on Earth? 
 

 
 
Step back again into the text, “forgive and you will be
forgiven…for the measure you give will be the measure you get back.” Jesus
invokes karma. That which you wish upon yourself, you must be that example. Even
more, this is a covenantal bond between you, God and the wider community. 
 

 
 
So yes, Many people think of the Bible as a guidebook
telling us what to do and not to do. If you do your best to follow them, that
might be all well and good. 
 

 
 
Again, I submit to you passages like this remind us there
is something more here. 
 
Wherever you are on the spectrum, the question is how do
you really participate in God’s kingdom?  Do you really embody what are
the stakes? (I don’t mean good juicy steak.) 
 

 
 
How do you live this, and how do you share this because
this is not meant to be a checklist so we can boast about our great work. This
is challenging us. 
 

 
 
Our order is being upended as we live just as order in
Jesus’s time was upended. Further, Jesus did not discriminate with people that
were different from his own culture or community. We have been given the grace
of God to be us and to live in our communities as faithful servants of our God while
living those precepts. When we do these in full body and mind, we may truly
receive grace. 
 

 
 
Perhaps today is the day to forgive those who hurt us so
badly.   Maybe now we can let go of that
pain in our lives.   
 
Perhaps today is the day we find out that we really do
have so much more we can give than just dollars and coins. 
 
Perhaps today is the day we reach out to the person in
our community that is needing a helping hand. 
 
Perhaps today is the day we say no to racial injustice, violence,
queer slurs or any bigotry so that we might instead embrace the whole world
that God gave us. 
 
Perhaps we can extend an authentic and genuine smile
because we would like that done to us. 
 

 
 
It has been done to us.  
 We have grace that has been given to us. Doesn’t that just warm your
hurt (even in the midst of all of this snow)? 
 

 
 
We could all just say we do these things (whether we do
or not) and say we live a moral and ethical life.  Jesus does not say this
just for oneself but how we are in the community. There is something more
here.  What is at stake is that God’s kingdom can be in the present now (and
not just as rewards for tomorrow.) 
 

 
 
A verse from another text can help us here. 
 

 
 
51b. 
 
Giving birth, 
 
Nourishing life, 
 
Shaping things without possessing them, 
 
Serving without expectation of rewards, 
 
Leading without dominating: 
 
These are the profound virtues of nature, 
 
And of nature’s best beings. 
 

 
 
“Love your enemies, do good and lend, expecting nothing in
return.   Your reward will be great and
you will be the children of the Most High.” (Luke 6: 35) 
 

 
 
Remember that we are in Epiphany.  In the beginning,
we talked about how God is revealing to us. Here, Jesus asks us how are we participating
in God’s kingdom – with all of God’s children. 
 

 
 
With this lesson, ask yourself How can you live your life
better each day by embodying God’s work here on Earth and you might see how
much grace you have been given. 
 

 
 
Let us be one with the spirit that surrounds us and bind
us. Let us be profound virtues of nature and let go of our expectations while
nourishing life and shaping the world which we live with our love of God. 
 

 
 
 As we prepare for
upcoming Lent (yes only couple weeks away), you could consider prohibitions
like abstaining from chocolates or something like that, and yes, I have my own
practice. This sermon from Jesus might serve as a template for this Lenten
journey. Yet for your Lenten journey, you don’t have to wait until then to

day. 
 

 
 
Thanks be to God!

<br />
<div class="MsoNormal">
I See You<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Tony E Hansen<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Reflection based upon Luke 5:1-11<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">Let us pray from Psalm 19, that words of my mouth and the
meditations of all of our hearts be acceptable.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">First, I want to thank you for spending this time with me
today.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>I have had an intense week of
work, and to be honest, being with you is somehow a reprieve from all of that.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>Thank you for your time and attendance
today.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">How many of you have heard about Perpetua and Justin Martyr? <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">Yes this is part of how get the word martyr. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">I have been reading a lot about the early Christian church (this
in addition to my work), <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">And caused me to ask what do perspectives of martyrdom teach us
today.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">I will share with one common thing that I found from these is
that despite an excruciating execution, <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">they share a understanding of faith that propelled and guided
them.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">They shared an implicit embrace of the spirit of Jesus in the
midst of certain death. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">My own toils and trials fall pale in comparison to these early
Christians -- as I am not sure what I would have done in those circumstances
(being persecuted and executed for my beliefs). <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">For us here in our own trials and life issues, maybe that spirit
of Jesus can inspire and empower us to have courage and strength, like those
martyrs before us. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">As I was thinking about the Gospel, I wanted to talk about being
a fisher of people, <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">but I don’t really know much about fishing as much as I have
tried. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">I even bought a whole array of equipment one time and went out
to the catch fish at the lake.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">I suppose it could be fun, <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">but I was kind of hoping to <i style="mso-bidi-font-style: normal;">will</i>
the fish into my cooler rather than wait for them.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">So I guess I am not a fisherman -- yet.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">Every time I say something like that, I have learned God has a
sense of humor about it. Someday, I may yet find myself in a boat (or otherwise)
fishing with actual results. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">There is also this curious thing about Jesus climbing into a
boat with Simon-Peter.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">Why does he do this? <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">Maybe, it is the crowd. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">What does Simon-Peter think about this?<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">We don’t have much context of how or if these two have met prior
to this. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";"><span style="mso-spacerun: yes;"> </span>It is not every day that
a random guy with a crowd following him decides to just jump into your boat. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">Think about it: <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">What would you do if a random guy or gal walked up to you and just
got into your car at the grocery store?<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">You might ask some questions and you might want to learn more
about this person.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">These guys do not reject Jesus, but they get into the boats with
Jesus and they listen. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">There is something here – not random.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">They realize something about Jesus. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">The next part of the lesson tells us what they realize. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">Let us dive into the verse here. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Simon-Peter exclaims, “Go away from me because I am a sinner”<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="background: white;">
<span style="color: #222222; mso-bidi-font-family: Calibri; mso-bidi-theme-font: minor-latin; mso-fareast-font-family: "Times New Roman";">This line definitely resonates with me, and I am sure with the
many of us. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Simon-Peter knows he is broken and feels unworthy of Jesus. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Where are you in this story? How many times have we thought
of ourselves as not being worthy because “I am a sinner?” <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Jesus persists and calls upon Simon-Peter and also calls
upon you and I.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>Why?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Traci Blackmon, UCC Executive Minister, talked to a group of
us last spring. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
She came in the room and stood there looking at us
intentionally and decisively.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Then, she said, “I see you!”<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;"> 
</span><o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
She wanted us to know that God sees us where we are today <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
--with everything we are and everything we can be. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
That is not always an easy thing to consider.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
We might go our whole lives wandering in the shadows with no
one paying attention.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>You might think
that about where you are currently. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
What happens when someone does pay attention? <o:p></o:p></div>

posts.text_content:
I See You 
 
Tony E Hansen 
 

 
 
Reflection based upon Luke 5:1-11 
 

 
 
 Let us pray from Psalm 19, that words of my mouth and the
meditations of all of our hearts be acceptable. 
 

 
 
 First, I want to thank you for spending this time with me
today.   I have had an intense week of
work, and to be honest, being with you is somehow a reprieve from all of that.   Thank you for your time and attendance
today.   
 

 
 
 How many of you have heard about Perpetua and Justin Martyr? 
 
 Yes this is part of how get the word martyr. 
 
 I have been reading a lot about the early Christian church (this
in addition to my work), 
 
 And caused me to ask what do perspectives of martyrdom teach us
today.   
 

 
 
 I will share with one common thing that I found from these is
that despite an excruciating execution, 
 
 they share a understanding of faith that propelled and guided
them.   
 
 They shared an implicit embrace of the spirit of Jesus in the
midst of certain death. 
 
 My own toils and trials fall pale in comparison to these early
Christians -- as I am not sure what I would have done in those circumstances
(being persecuted and executed for my beliefs). 
 

 
 
 For us here in our own trials and life issues, maybe that spirit
of Jesus can inspire and empower us to have courage and strength, like those
martyrs before us. 
 

 
 
 As I was thinking about the Gospel, I wanted to talk about being
a fisher of people, 
 
 but I don’t really know much about fishing as much as I have
tried. 
 
 I even bought a whole array of equipment one time and went out
to the catch fish at the lake.   
 
 I suppose it could be fun, 
 
 but I was kind of hoping to will 
the fish into my cooler rather than wait for them.   
 
 So I guess I am not a fisherman -- yet.   
 

 
 
 Every time I say something like that, I have learned God has a
sense of humor about it. Someday, I may yet find myself in a boat (or otherwise)
fishing with actual results. 
 

 
 
 There is also this curious thing about Jesus climbing into a
boat with Simon-Peter.   
 
 Why does he do this? 
 
 Maybe, it is the crowd. 
 
 What does Simon-Peter think about this?   
 
 We don’t have much context of how or if these two have met prior
to this. 
 
   It is not every day that
a random guy with a crowd following him decides to just jump into your boat. 
 

 
 
 Think about it: 
 
 What would you do if a random guy or gal walked up to you and just
got into your car at the grocery store?   
 
 You might ask some questions and you might want to learn more
about this person. 
 

 
 
 These guys do not reject Jesus, but they get into the boats with
Jesus and they listen. 
 
 There is something here – not random.   
 
 They realize something about Jesus. 
 

 
 
 The next part of the lesson tells us what they realize. 
 
 Let us dive into the verse here. 
 

 
 
Simon-Peter exclaims, “Go away from me because I am a sinner” 
 

 
 
 This line definitely resonates with me, and I am sure with the
many of us. 
 

 
 
Simon-Peter knows he is broken and feels unworthy of Jesus. 
 

 
 
Where are you in this story? How many times have we thought
of ourselves as not being worthy because “I am a sinner?” 
 

 
 
Jesus persists and calls upon Simon-Peter and also calls
upon you and I.   Why? 
 

 
 
Traci Blackmon, UCC Executive Minister, talked to a group of
us last spring. 
 
She came in the room and stood there looking at us
intentionally and decisively.   
 
Then, she said, “I see you!”  
 
 
She wanted us to know that God sees us where we are today 
 
--with everything we are and everything we can be. 
 
That is not always an easy thing to consider.   
 

 
 
We might go our whole lives wandering in the shadows with no
one paying attention.   You might think
that about where you are currently. 
 

 
 
What happens when someone does pay attention? 
 
That is happening now. 
 
You may ask God sees me?? 
 
Today? 
 
God wants this? Why? 
 

 
 
Yet Jesus saw Simon-Peter. Why? 
 
Maybe, Jesus has more faith in Simon-Peter does in
himself.   
 
In the same way, God sees you. 
 

 
 
Jesus wants us to be the best we can be with the gifts we
have. 
 
Jesus will be there with us always and gives us even more.   
 
Jesus inspires the best in us to shine through us – when you
be what God calls you to be. 
 
When you let your heart shine, you are what God calls. 
 

 
 
We like to think the reverse – 
 
that religion is about telling us what we cannot do 
 
and things we must do to earn our way to life with God.   
 
There are valid arguments with this because our thoughts can
lead us astray.   
 
Our actions can put us onto a path that separates us from
the holy. 
 
Yet, I submit that we are exactly what God made us since we
are made in the image of God. 
 

 
 
It took a while for me to understand my wrongs and
brokenness; 
 
they don’t have to define me.   
 
If we do let wrongs and brokenness define us, 
 
we just might be separating ourselves from what we could be
-- from God. 
 
We might not even get into the boat with God 
 

 
 
We don’t have to continue “stinkin’ thinking” (Zig
Ziglar).   
 
These bits of brokenness, however, can inform us as lessons
but they do not have to define us.   
 

 
 
   God is there for us
always and regardless of our brokenness. 
 
   God sees you and
wants you!   
 

 
 
What happens here is that Jesus rejects Simon-Peter’s
self-effacing 
 
and instead says “I see you.” 
 
I see   who you are and
who you could be. I see you. (look around) 
 

 
 
God is ready to inspire you too, here and now. 
 

 
 
So maybe like Simon-Peter’s words, we might feel unworthy,
but God calls us to be worthy. 
 
It was not easy, but these new disciples let God be their
guide. 
 

 
 
We may not be martyrs destined for painful execution because
of our beliefs, 
 
but the spirit and grace can be powerful in its own right --
for us here and now.   
 
The spirit is all around and God sees you. I see you. 
 

 
 
We may not be good fishermen, 
 
but we might realize and take solace in that God calls to be
who we are. 
 
It is up to us to recognize that grace and let us be us –
let God be – let God guide us. 
 

 
 
In fact, I submit that grace is right here, and we will see
it when we take time to see it. 
 
Our purpose, gifts, and our brokenness are exactly why God
chooses us. 
 

 
 
Thanks be to God!

<br />
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">When
I read versions of the Nicene creed, I am drawn to memory of the way I recited the
creed as a profession of faith in the Catholic Mass.  I am drawn also to
the rosary and how we would use that as a variation of meditative prayer. 
We say these things over and over in order to foster a sense of reverence, and
I can still verbatim recite each prayer and the profession that we learned
then.  That is a unique way to do meditation by reciting common phrases
and prayers -- and a great way to learn them.  Since I do not fully
subscribe to the Nicene or Apostles Creed these days, I look for other ways
that might describe how I believe without being constrained to them. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<br />
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Today,
I turn to the Tao Te Ching and ask which is so important that I would want to
incorporate that into my meditation rather than as an empty mind or mindfulness
meditation. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Since
the Nicene creed calls God into being through Jesus Christ and the holy Spirit,
I am drawn to particular verses that talks about being born and into being. Let
us meditate upon being.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">40b<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"> “Returning
to the root is the movement of the Tao.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Quietness
is how it functions.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Ten
thousand things are born of being.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Being
is born of nonbeing. “<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">42a<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">“Nonbeing
gives birth to the oneness,<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">The
oneness gives birth to yin and yang.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Yin
and yang give birth to heaven, earth, and beings.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Heaven,
earth, and beings give birth to everything in existence.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Therefore,
everything in existence carries within it both yin and yang,<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">and
attains harmony by blending these…”<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Meditating
on this, I feel the different dimensions of God.  Perhaps, others also
might feel and see the different dimensions of God working with us and around
us as trinity, God and spirit or as spirit or as Jesus. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">The
power of God perhaps can be described, but like the words of the Tao, words
cannot contain God. From God, the onenness, "maker ...of all that is seen
and unseen", we have the spirit, Jesus and beautiful beings in Heaven and
Earth.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">What
this tells me in this meditative reflection is that whether Jesus was God
incarnate, "God from God, true light from true light, begotten not
made," a divine being created by God as an intercession to us, or a person
with strong connection to God "by the power of the Holy Spirit",
Jesus's work here on Earth, "for our sake... was crucified ...suffered,
died..." is a powerful testament of Truth.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">How
do we live out our testament of Truth? That we all are born of and made of the
work of God that binds us to the being of God and how we work with each other
is important. When I meditate on these, I can feel how God is of the yin and
yang as we are in this world that has been gifted to us. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">In
fact, Jesus teaches a version of the yin and yang and to find contentment
rather than to persist in expectations through the sermon on the plain that we
read during  the weeks of lectionary in Luke.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">51b.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Giving
birth,<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Nourishing
life,<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Shaping
things without possessing them,<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Serving
without expectation of rewards,<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Leading
without dominating:<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">These
are the profound virtues of nature,<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">And
of nature’s best beings.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">“Love
your enemies, do good and lend, expecting nothing in return.  Your reward
will be great and you will be the children of the Most High.” (Luke 6: 35)<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Let
us be one with the Spirit, "the giver of life", that surrounds us and
binds us. Let us be profound virtues of nature and expect nothing in return
while nourishing life and shaping the world we live with our love .<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Amen.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">

<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">*As
translated by Brown Walker, B. (1995). The Tao Te Ching of Lao Tzu. First St.
Martin’s Griffin Ed: New York.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;"><br /></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal" style="mso-margin-bottom-alt: auto; mso-margin-top-alt: auto;">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Then, </span></div>
<br />
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Reading the material around Dionysius, it is fitting we might read
this on the week of Transfiguration Sunday with such a mystical stories of Jesus
and Moses. I again sense Taoism and parts of the Tao Te Ching, but this time, I
would like to meditate on the principles of the duality very present in Dionysius work: the opposites as they
all form as part of the one. <o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Let our spirit rise and fall with this meditation.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">From the Book of Chuang Tzu (translated by Martin Palmer p
188)<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">“Life Follows death and death is the forerunner of life.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Who can know their ways?...<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">As death and life are together in all this, which can be
termed bad? All the forms of life are one…, yet we regard some as beautiful …others
as ugly… but even the diseased and rotting can become the spiritual and
wonderful, and the spiritual and wonderful can become the diseased and rotting.
“<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">The mysticism of this weaves with the Dionysius line into
this discussion: “outshining all brilliance with the intensity of their
Darkness” and then, “yet in a ..sense, it does not possess them since it
transcends them all;”<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Thus, we witness transcendence from left to right and light
to dark.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">We see transcendence from right to left and dark to light;<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">From death to life and life to death.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Out of darkness came light and from light we go to darkness.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">All are one with the presence of the Holy One, the Divine
Wisdom.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">And suddenly transfiguration is a transcendence that we can
witness in our own lives.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">With the “One who is beyond all”, we cannot literally
comprehend that infinite image who embodies both the divine light and the
Darkness to reveal the naked Truth: that we cannot speak it because we cannot
describe it, but we can know it.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">How do we allow the light and darkness to transcend within
us and in our being? How do we reject the perfect light and darkness by our feeble
attempt to define its trueness, its being?<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Spirit of the living God fall upon us and be with us in all
of your splendor and murky ways.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Spirit of the One who gives us life and death, be nearer to
our understanding and our denials.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Reveal to us so we might be able to truly embrace what we
cannot describe and allow that to be the naked Truth in our lives.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">Spirit of the light and the Dark, be far from us so that we
might be comforted in your presence.<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">That we may continue yours in no-words language,
actionless-action and thinkingless-thought,<o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">And through your holy Spirit, open our questions and hearts
to your True presence.<o:p></o:p></span></div>

posts.text_content:
When
I read versions of the Nicene creed, I am drawn to memory of the way I recited the
creed as a profession of faith in the Catholic Mass.  I am drawn also to
the rosary and how we would use that as a variation of meditative prayer. 
We say these things over and over in order to foster a sense of reverence, and
I can still verbatim recite each prayer and the profession that we learned
then.  That is a unique way to do meditation by reciting common phrases
and prayers -- and a great way to learn them.  Since I do not fully
subscribe to the Nicene or Apostles Creed these days, I look for other ways
that might describe how I believe without being constrained to them.  
 
 
 

 
 Today,
I turn to the Tao Te Ching and ask which is so important that I would want to
incorporate that into my meditation rather than as an empty mind or mindfulness
meditation.  
 
 Since
the Nicene creed calls God into being through Jesus Christ and the holy Spirit,
I am drawn to particular verses that talks about being born and into being. Let
us meditate upon being. 
 
 
 
 
 40b 
 
  “Returning
to the root is the movement of the Tao. 
 
 Quietness
is how it functions. 
 
 Ten
thousand things are born of being. 
 
 Being
is born of nonbeing. “ 
 
 
 
 
 42a 
 
 “Nonbeing
gives birth to the oneness, 
 
 The
oneness gives birth to yin and yang. 
 
 Yin
and yang give birth to heaven, earth, and beings. 
 
 Heaven,
earth, and beings give birth to everything in existence. 
 
 Therefore,
everything in existence carries within it both yin and yang, 
 
 and
attains harmony by blending these…” 
 
 
 
 
 Meditating
on this, I feel the different dimensions of God.  Perhaps, others also
might feel and see the different dimensions of God working with us and around
us as trinity, God and spirit or as spirit or as Jesus.  
 
 
 
 
 The
power of God perhaps can be described, but like the words of the Tao, words
cannot contain God. From God, the onenness, "maker ...of all that is seen
and unseen", we have the spirit, Jesus and beautiful beings in Heaven and
Earth. 
 
 
 
 
 What
this tells me in this meditative reflection is that whether Jesus was God
incarnate, "God from God, true light from true light, begotten not
made," a divine being created by God as an intercession to us, or a person
with strong connection to God "by the power of the Holy Spirit",
Jesus's work here on Earth, "for our sake... was crucified ...suffered,
died..." is a powerful testament of Truth. 
 
 
 
 
 How
do we live out our testament of Truth? That we all are born of and made of the
work of God that binds us to the being of God and how we work with each other
is important. When I meditate on these, I can feel how God is of the yin and
yang as we are in this world that has been gifted to us.  
 
 In
fact, Jesus teaches a version of the yin and yang and to find contentment
rather than to persist in expectations through the sermon on the plain that we
read during  the weeks of lectionary in Luke. 
 
 
 
 
 51b. 
 
 Giving
birth, 
 
 Nourishing
life, 
 
 Shaping
things without possessing them, 
 
 Serving
without expectation of rewards, 
 
 Leading
without dominating: 
 
 These
are the profound virtues of nature, 
 
 And
of nature’s best beings. 
 
 
 
 
 “Love
your enemies, do good and lend, expecting nothing in return.  Your reward
will be great and you will be the children of the Most High.” (Luke 6: 35) 
 
 
 
 
 Let
us be one with the Spirit, "the giver of life", that surrounds us and
binds us. Let us be profound virtues of nature and expect nothing in return
while nourishing life and shaping the world we live with our love . 
 
 Amen. 
 

 

 
 
 

 

 
 
 *As
translated by Brown Walker, B. (1995). The Tao Te Ching of Lao Tzu. First St.
Martin’s Griffin Ed: New York. 
 
 
 
 
 Then,  

 
 Reading the material around Dionysius, it is fitting we might read
this on the week of Transfiguration Sunday with such a mystical stories of Jesus
and Moses. I again sense Taoism and parts of the Tao Te Ching, but this time, I
would like to meditate on the principles of the duality very present in Dionysius work: the opposites as they
all form as part of the one.  
 

 
 
 Let our spirit rise and fall with this meditation. 
 

 
 
 From the Book of Chuang Tzu (translated by Martin Palmer p
188) 
 
 “Life Follows death and death is the forerunner of life. 
 
 Who can know their ways?... 
 
 As death and life are together in all this, which can be
termed bad? All the forms of life are one…, yet we regard some as beautiful …others
as ugly… but even the diseased and rotting can become the spiritual and
wonderful, and the spiritual and wonderful can become the diseased and rotting.
“ 
 

 
 
 The mysticism of this weaves with the Dionysius line into
this discussion: “outshining all brilliance with the intensity of their
Darkness” and then, “yet in a ..sense, it does not possess them since it
transcends them all;” 
 

 
 
 Thus, we witness transcendence from left to right and light
to dark. 
 
 We see transcendence from right to left and dark to light; 
 
 From death to life and life to death. 
 
 Out of darkness came light and from light we go to darkness. 
 
 All are one with the presence of the Holy One, the Divine
Wisdom. 
 

 
 
 And suddenly transfiguration is a transcendence that we can
witness in our own lives. 
 
 With the “One who is beyond all”, we cannot literally
comprehend that infinite image who embodies both the divine light and the
Darkness to reveal the naked Truth: that we cannot speak it because we cannot
describe it, but we can know it. 
 

 
 
 How do we allow the light and darkness to transcend within
us and in our being? How do we reject the perfect light and darkness by our feeble
attempt to define its trueness, its being? 
 

 
 
 Spirit of the living God fall upon us and be with us in all
of your splendor and murky ways. 
 
 Spirit of the One who gives us life and death, be nearer to
our understanding and our denials. 
 
 Reveal to us so we might be able to truly embrace what we
cannot describe and allow that to be the naked Truth in our lives. 
 

 
 
 Spirit of the light and the Dark, be far from us so that we
might be comforted in your presence. 
 
 That we may continue yours in no-words language,
actionless-action and thinkingless-thought, 
 
 And through your holy Spirit, open our questions and hearts
to your True presence.

posts.text_content:
Reflecting upon St Francis

 
 
 
Tony E Hansen 
 

 
 
I have fondness for St Francis of Assisi due to going to
Mass at a church bearing his name for many years and that he is renown for love
of nature as stewards of God’s creation. Statues of his image are usually
adorned with birds and small animals.  
 The two that we have do not have these, which, in our eyes, gives us a
glimpse of his inner humility that also shows some of the poverty of which he
lived deliberately. It is with this image that I see most profound in the
current Pope in Rome. 
 

 
 
St Francis, like Hildegard with sexuality, venerate the
absence of something in their lives. For Francis, this is primarily material
wealth. This is in stark contrast to the growing abuses of many in the Catholic
church at the time (and actually continues to this day in all of the Christian Church.)   Yet he also duly venerates the sacraments and
people that “honor above all things”. 
 

 
 
 nother goal of Francis is also absence of
idleness. So, it is fitting that I come upon this reading and study of Francis
in spring and as we begin to prepare our yard with gardening and landscapes. 
 
 
 

 
 
Here, I can understand what Francis means by honest job and
working with hands 
 
Here, let us pray together over the work to be and what God
is saying to us in that work. 
 

 
 
 

 

 
 
The Lord give you peace. 
 
From the work of our hands, 
 
we feel Your spirit within this earth and these stones 
 
As if they were crying out to You, oh Lord. 
 

 
 
From the creation You made for us, 
 
let us be mindful of Your purpose in the space 
 
And in the spaces between those spaces as when You cry out
to us. 
 

 
 
From the movement in this space, 
 
we are moved with Your presence and inspiration 
 
As when You guided our brother Francis. 
 

 
 
From the listening as we glorify your creation, 
 
we are called to be your servants in duty, in mind and work 
 
As always Your children on this earth . 
 

 
 
From You touching and nudging, 
 
We are called to feel the work of those around the world
forming within these tools 
 
As we put them to Your work in Your Creation. 
 

 
 
From Your laughing spirit You join us, 
 
We rejoice with friends, spirits and contemplation 
 
As You come to share Your love, so shall we. 
 

 
 
From Your presence and wisdom 
 
We are called to share these gifts of our work because they
were blessed by You. 
 
As duly consecrated by You and guided by brother Francis. 
 

 
 
We are reminded in this good work of the spirit of communion
 
 
Of which you call us together in work and in celebration of
Your gifts to us 
 
Whether in this space or in our in community,   
 
we work with our hands to be stewards of Your Creation and Your
Children. 
 
May the Lord give us peace.

<div class="MsoNormal">
Woe to contentment: Our work is not yet done.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Tony E Hansen<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Reflection based upon Luke 13:31-35; Psalm 27; Genesis 15:17<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Let us be in state of prayer. From Psalm 19, May the words
of my mouth and the meditations of all of our hearts be acceptable in your
sight O Lord You are our rock and our Redeemer!<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Happy Lent!!<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
In this time of Lent, we are positioned to reflect and think
about our lives, what we miss, and what we could improve.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
As we continue on this journey through Lent , you could still
consider prohibitions -- like abstaining from chocolates, Facebook, adult
beverages, swearing (I have heard some of you and you know who you are) or
something like that. Yes, I have my own practice. If you have one, great! if
you don’t, I would like for you to consider adding something to your lives this
season. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
I submit to you to review and consider with me the sermon
on the plain to serve as guideposts for our journey this year.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>As I was working with the text, I saw the
potential for gifts and focus points for each week -- even each day.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>I hope you will as well.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNoSpacing">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
So let us consider our current lesson that talks about this
conversation with Jesus and put that in context of first part of that sermon on
the plain. <span style="mso-spacerun: yes;"> </span>So the question to ask is, what
does a fox, the city of Jerusalem and woes have in common?<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>(In my goofy, dry sense of humor, that starts
to sound like the beginning of a good joke.)<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Let the spirit move us as it did Jesus.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Jesus is approached by some Pharisees that “warn” Jesus about
Herod. This is kind of interesting, in of itself, because we have a set of
elites warning Jesus about other elites. In the words of Robin Hood, as played
by the wise Daffy Duck, “somethings amiss here.”<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
What does Jesus do? Calls out the boloney. Then tells them
and all present, I am on my mission (ministry) and no one will prevent me from
doing God’s work.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>Further, you may not
recognize Jesus’s work as it happens, but soon enough you will. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
In this passage, we see one of Luke’s chief concerns is that
of hypocrisy.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>Here, Jesus laments over
people’s attitudes towards the hypocrisy of the political elites, the religious
elites here and the people who contently follow them. What is Jesus saying to
us?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
That might be best explained when we look back a few
chapters -- using our section of the sermon on plain. Last week, our group
walked together through first part of this Lenten journey through the sermon on
the plain.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>Allow me to recap.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
We reviewed some of the beatitudes (blessed are the poor and
the meek, for your reward is coming) essentially can be summarized to three
points:<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
1)Blessed are you who seek the Truth! 2) Trust in God 3)
because you are not alone.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Further that reward is the kingdom of God. I submit to you
that God does not want us to wait until death to participate.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Jesus’s sermon on the level place then brings us to some
woes. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="line" style="background: white; line-height: 18.0pt; margin-bottom: .0001pt; margin: 0in;">
“…<span class="text"><span style="color: black; font-family: "helvetica neue";">woe to you who are rich,</span></span><span style="color: black; font-family: "helvetica neue";"><br />
</span><span class="indent-1-breaks"><span style="color: black; font-family: "courier new"; font-size: 5.0pt;">    </span></span><span class="text"><span style="color: black; font-family: "helvetica neue";">…who are full
now,</span></span><span style="color: black; font-family: "helvetica neue";"><br />
</span><span class="indent-1-breaks"><span style="color: black; font-family: "courier new"; font-size: 5.0pt;">    </span></span><span class="text"><span style="color: black; font-family: "helvetica neue";">for you will
be hungry.</span></span><span style="color: black; font-family: "helvetica neue";"><br />
<span class="text">“…you who are laughing now,</span><br />
</span><span class="indent-1-breaks"><span style="color: black; font-family: "courier new"; font-size: 5.0pt;">    </span></span><span class="text"><span style="color: black; font-family: "helvetica neue";">for you will …
weep.</span></span><span style="color: black; font-family: "helvetica neue";"><o:p></o:p></span></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
What are these woes? Woes against pleasure, no! These are
woes against contentment.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>Yes, we are
blessed when we seek and trust in God, but we must be careful not to fall into
the trap of contentment because contentment is a fleeting illusion.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>In fact, contentment can lead to a form of
idolatry rather than as venerating certain icons, money or personal success,
but we are want to let these and worldly treasures prevent us from continuing
to do what we are called to do.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
We have this throughout our lives, and I have a few examples
where I have fallen short on this notion. Let me illustrate one.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
I was reminded of this when watching the film <i style="mso-bidi-font-style: normal;">Christopher Robin</i> (a story about the
Pooh, Tigger and Eeyore characters and the Hundred Acres Woods.) When I, as a
father, am called to be a father for Tyler or to be a spouse to my love, yet when
work calls, I too often felt compelled to switch gears and that became my focus
for a day, evening or weekend. How many times have I missed something because I
just did not do what I was called to do over an presumption of importance: an
illusion of importance.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>Even recently, I
found myself in the middle of a project go-live and working an over-abundance
of overtime to see successful objectives.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;"> 
</span>Yet, at what cost?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
To consider this even more the irony is that it might have
been easier to spend time with my family “doing nothing” than spend time
anchored to my desk.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>Perhaps it is
necessary. Perhaps that is the purpose of holidays – even Jesus reminds us to take
time for ourselves.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
To counter these outside forces, I have intentionally
enforced boundaries on these so that I might fulfill my promise and my call.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
This is, however, more than just following through on a
promise<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
It could have been easy for Jesus to hear the warning from
the Pharisees here and stop what the mission and ministry, but that is not what
God called of Jesus to do. Similarly, it could be easy for me or you to ignore
truths in our society, especially when someone raises a potential warning and abandoned
what we are called to do as followers of Christ.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>That might be safe, that might be the
compelling thing to do, but is it safe and is it worth our attention?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Why be content with saying the good words and then doing
nothing with it? Why be content with just sitting in church when God calls us
to do so much more.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>We cannot be content
with things because then we become the Jerusalem that Jesus laments -- while
the fox takes from us, hides from and abuses power.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
When you feel content with your Christian call today, you
risk leaving the best part of yourself sitting in that pew when you leave
worship and you risk not participating in God’s kingdom. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
So What are we called to do that we are content ignoring?
What are we substituting for what we are called to do; what God calls us to do?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Let us listen for a moment to some suggestions.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Over the past few years, I have grown quite a bit more faith
in our youth. In fact, I would say that they have re-invigorated some of my
work in the public sphere, and the youth are genuinely exciting me to do work!<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
The youth over the past few years have been calling out the
fallacy of a broken system that seems designed to quiet us.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span>Perhaps this is one reason why Jesus calls upon
us to listen to children because they have not understood our cultural
ignorance as their own. Recently, they have been calling us to a truth with no
place for contentment for what <i style="mso-bidi-font-style: normal;">we</i>
think is “normal.”<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Is it really ok to feel numb to another school
shooting?<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Is it really ok to ruin God’s creation: our Earth: their
future home?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Is it really ok to deny someone their justice, fairness or
equality, whether immigrant, queer, black or blue?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Is it really ok to ignore the PTSD of honorable men and
women returning from wars?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Is it really ok to be <i style="mso-bidi-font-style: normal;">that</i>
normal?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
The youth are compelling us to look at where we are -- just
as Jesus does in these two pieces.<span style="mso-spacerun: yes;">  </span><o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
They are calling out the fox and calling out Jerusalem -
less we be that fox.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Let me put it another way.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
My mother taught me a lesson once that when you move out of
an apartment or house to leave it in better condition than we received it. Can
we say that about our world and our youth – when we are content with “it is
what it is”?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
We, who do nothing, to prepare our world for them better
than we received it do nothing to help our youth.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Perhaps, instead of busying ourselves with who should not be
part of our community,<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Perhaps, instead of nodding to rhetoric and ego, or violence
as a way of life<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Perhaps instead of forgetting what we are call to do<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Perhaps instead of finding excuses to put off to tomorrow,<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Perhaps then we do what the youth are calling us to do !<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Perhaps then we do the work that is our mission as
Christians – no matter who you are or where you are on life’s journey.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
We do not have to agree on everything but we don’t have to argue
over the scraps dropped from the table of power.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
We do not have to make excuses for them.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Like Christopher Robin, we can remember who we are and why
we are here.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
What is truly important in our lives is not just facades or
worldly treasures, <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
But what God calls us to do for ourselves, our family, and
our world.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
No we don’t have to fight over scraps, rhetoric and illusions.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Let us listen to our youth.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
I see the good Lord working through them and filling us with
hope <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
That has long been forgotten. <o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
We can be what God has invited us to be and to do his good
work.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Again, Blessed are those who seek the Truth<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Trust in God<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Because you are not Alone.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Be mindful of contentment because<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
God is calling you to continue the good work.<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
“Blessed is the one who comes in the name off the Lord.”
Luke 13:35<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Is that you?<o:p></o:p></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
<br /></div>
<div class="MsoNormal">
Thanks be to God!</div>
